objective: Resolve the nine high findings grype reports for the container image's build-time and runtime-tool packages, so the supply-chain scan reports the real state of the image instead of failing on packages that are not reachable.
decision_supported: Can the container scan be made honest without lowering any gate — that is, without changing severity-cutoff, disabling fail-build, or adding a blanket VEX entry?
acceptance: The lock resolves with --require-hashes after moving virtualenv to 21.15.1 and filelock to 4.2.4, and both import.
Every high finding in the grype report names the exact purl the report emitted in docker/vex.json, with a justification and an impact statement that carries the evidence.
No change to severity-cutoff, fail-build, or the scan action itself.
tests/unit/test_container_profiles.py enumerates the VEX (vulnerability, purl) set so a blanket ignore entry fails.
evidence: workbench-1-grype.json from run 40643503777: severity High 9, of which 8 are virtualenv/filelock pinned in docker/requirements-dev.lock and 1 is @fastify/busboy vendored inside Ubuntu Noble's nodejs.
Installing the updated lock into a scratch --target with --require-hashes resolves and both packages import at their new versions.
stop_conditions: The scan still reports a high finding that is reachable at run time; that would need a real upgrade or removal, not a VEX statement.
nodejs turns out to be needed for something other than the in-image accessibility tests; removing it would then be possible and preferable to a VEX statement.
risks_and_fallbacks: A VEX statement is an assertion about reachability, so each one names the purl and the reason rather than only a status.
The lock upgrade changes two build-time tools; if the frozen set was chosen deliberately, the hashes and versions are the only change and the rest of the lock is untouched.
